kurals.tamil:
தக்காங்கு நாடித் தலைச்செல்லா வண்ணத்தால்
ஒத்தாங்கு ஒறுப்பது வேந்து.
kurals.transliteration:
Thakkaangu naadith thalaichchellaa vannaththaal
Oththaangu oruppadhu vaendhu.
kurals.meaning: A true king first investigates a wrong fairly and thoroughly, and then punishes it in a measure that fits the offence, so that it is not repeated.
kurals.elementary: Imagine a teacher who finds a broken window. A good teacher first finds out calmly who did it and why, and then gives a fair consequence, not too big and not too small, so it won't happen again. This kural says a good ruler works the same way: find out the truth first, then correct fairly.
kurals.university: The chapter title வெருவந்த செய்யாமை means ‘not doing things that cause dread (veru)’, and Valluvar opens it not by forbidding punishment but by defining its right form. Three steps are packed into the couplet: தக்காங்கு நாடி (investigating as is fitting, i.e., impartially), ஒத்தாங்கு ஒறுத்தல் (punishing in a measure that matches the offence), and the purpose clause தலைச்செல்லா வண்ணத்தால் (so that the wrong does not advance or recur). The traditional commentators, with Parimelazhagar at their head, read this as the positive standard against which the tyranny of the previous chapter (கொடுங்கோன்மை, ch. 56) is measured, and modern glosses (Mu. Varadarasanar, Solomon Pappaiah, Kalaignar) all stress neutrality in inquiry and proportion in penalty. The definition-style ending ‘… வேந்து’ (‘that is a king’) makes proportionate justice constitutive of kingship itself. Text agrees across ytamizh.com and thirukkural-thamizh.org, the latter printing the older sandhi-joined form (வண்ணத்தா / லொத்தாங் கொறுப்பது) with no change in wording.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “If (punishment) is properly inflicted after (due) consideration, it makes all people happy; but inflicted without consideration, it destroys everything.”
hinduism.explanation: Manu teaches that danda (punishment) is a blessing only when applied after careful examination; used rashly, it ruins the whole order it is meant to protect.
hinduism.tie_back: Both texts insist that investigation must come before punishment, exactly the Kural’s ‘தக்காங்கு நாடி’.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Very close on due consideration; Manu does not state the deterrent purpose as explicitly as the Kural.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Doth our law judge any man, before it hear him, and know what he doeth?”
christianity.explanation: Nicodemus reminds the council that the law forbids condemning anyone before a hearing and a proper inquiry into what he has done.
christianity.tie_back: Nicodemus’s principle of hearing before judging is the first step the Kural requires of a king.
christianity._accuracy_note: Matches the investigation step only; the proportionality and deterrence elements are absent.

islam.quote_or_event: “And if you punish [an enemy, O believers], punish with an equivalent of that with which you were harmed. But if you are patient - it is better for those who are patient.”
islam.explanation: The Quran allows retribution only in strict equivalence to the harm done, and praises restraint above even that.
islam.tie_back: The Kural’s ‘ஒத்தாங்கு ஒறுத்தல்’ (punishing in matching measure) is the same principle of equivalence.
islam._accuracy_note: Strong on proportion; the verse addresses retaliation by the wronged rather than a king’s judicial inquiry.

judaism.quote_or_event: “And the judges shall make diligent inquisition … And those which remain shall hear, and fear, and shall henceforth commit no more any such evil among you.”
judaism.explanation: Deuteronomy requires judges to investigate diligently, and gives the purpose of the penalty as preventing the evil from being repeated.
judaism.tie_back: Diligent inquiry plus a penalty aimed at non-recurrence is almost exactly ‘தக்காங்கு நாடித் தலைச்செல்லா வண்ணத்தால்’.
judaism._accuracy_note: Near one-to-one on inquiry and deterrence; the specific case is false witness, not crime in general.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “It is my desire that there should be uniformity in law and uniformity in sentencing.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddhist emperor Ashoka ordered his judicial officers (rajjukas) to judge consistently and even granted a three-day stay to those sentenced to death so appeals could be heard.
buddhism.tie_back: Ashoka’s even-handed, reviewable sentencing is a royal program for the Kural’s fair, fitting punishment.
buddhism.source: Ashoka, Pillar Edict IV (trans. S. Dhammika)
buddhism._accuracy_note: Good match on consistent, measured justice; the edict says less about the deterrent aim.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In Greek myth Rhadamanthys, famed for his strict fairness, judges the dead; Plato’s Gorgias imagines souls judged stripped of rank and finery so that the judge sees each soul exactly as it is.
greek_mythology.explanation: The myth makes the ideal judge one who examines the true character of each case without being swayed by status.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The Kural’s demand for impartial investigation before punishment is personified in Rhadamanthys.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Fits the impartial-inquiry idea; it concerns afterlife judgment, not a king’s proportionate penalties.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “But he who desires to inflict rational punishment does not retaliate for a past wrong which cannot be undone; he has regard to the future, and is desirous that the man who is punished, and he who sees him punished, may be deterred from doing wrong again.”
philosophy.explanation: Protagoras argues that rational punishment looks forward, aiming to prevent repetition rather than to vent anger over the past.
philosophy.tie_back: This is the Kural’s purpose clause ‘தலைச்செல்லா வண்ணத்தால்’, punishing so that the wrong does not recur.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Excellent on deterrent purpose; Protagoras does not stress investigation or proportion.

kurals.tamil:
கடிதோச்சி மெல்ல எறிக நெடிதாக்கம்
நீங்காமை வேண்டு பவர்.
kurals.transliteration:
Kadidhoachchi mella eriga nedidhaakkam
Neengaamai vaendu bavar.
kurals.meaning: Rulers who want their prosperity to last long should raise the rod sternly but let it fall gently: firm in warning, mild in the actual penalty.
kurals.elementary: Think of a parent who says in a serious voice, ‘If you do that again, there will be no TV for a month!’, but when it happens, takes away TV for just one evening. The warning is strong, the punishment is gentle. The kural says leaders who do this keep their people’s trust for a long time.
kurals.university: The image is of a raised stick: கடிது ஓச்சி (lift it high, severely) but மெல்ல எறிக (bring it down softly). The classical commentary, followed by Mu. Varadarasanar, reads this as appearing to proceed with great severity while in fact not exceeding due measure, while Kalaignar’s modern gloss separates the stages as stern reproof but mild punishment. The reward named is நெடிது ஆக்கம் நீங்காமை, prosperity that does not depart for a long time, so the couplet argues from prudence as much as from mercy. Pope’s ‘raise the rod with brow severe, but let it gently fall’ has become the standard English rendering. thirukkural-thamizh.org prints the sandhi form ‘மெல்ல வெறிக’, which is the same words as ‘மெல்ல எறிக’.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “No,” says Kauṭilya; for whoever imposes severe punishment becomes repulsive to the people; while he who awards mild punishment becomes contemptible. But whoever imposes punishment as deserved becomes respectable.
hinduism.explanation: Kautilya rejects his teacher’s advice that a king should always hold the sceptre raised (udyatadaṇḍa), arguing for punishment that is deserved, neither harsh nor lax.
hinduism.tie_back: The raised-but-restrained sceptre in the Arthashastra is the same picture as the Kural’s rod raised high but lowered gently.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Both contrast the raised rod with measured use; Kautilya argues for ‘as deserved’ rather than explicitly ‘gentle’.

christianity.quote_or_event: “For he shall have judgment without mercy, that hath shewed no mercy; and mercy rejoiceth against judgment.”
christianity.explanation: James teaches that judgment stays real but mercy has the final word over it.
christianity.tie_back: The rod is raised (judgment) but comes down gently (mercy), which is the Kural’s balance.
christianity._accuracy_note: Captures mercy tempering judgment; James speaks of divine judgment, not a ruler’s policy or long prosperity.

islam.quote_or_event: “Avert the legal penalties from the Muslims as much as possible, if he has a way out then leave him to his way, for if the Imam makes a mistake in forgiving it would be better than making mistake in punishment.”
islam.explanation: This narration keeps the fixed penalties on the books but urges the ruler to avoid applying them wherever a way out exists.
islam.tie_back: Severe law, lenient application: the rod is raised high but falls softly.
islam._accuracy_note: Strong thematic fit; sunnah.com notes the chain is graded Da'if (weak), though the principle is widely accepted in Islamic law.

judaism.quote_or_event: The Mishnah records that a Sanhedrin which executes someone once in seven years is called destructive; Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya says once in seventy years, and Rabbis Tarfon and Akiva say that had they sat on the Sanhedrin no one would ever have been executed.
judaism.explanation: The rabbis kept capital law in the Torah but surrounded it with procedures so demanding that it was almost never carried out.
judaism.tie_back: Stern law held high, applied with extreme restraint, is the Jewish legal form of the Kural’s gentle stroke.
judaism._accuracy_note: Paraphrased, not quoted; a close structural match, though the rabbis’ concern is sanctity of life rather than royal prosperity.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “They are told that despite his remorse Beloved-of-the-Gods has the power to punish them if necessary, so that they should be ashamed of their wrong and not be killed.”
buddhism.explanation: After Kalinga, Ashoka reminded restless forest peoples that he still held the power to punish, precisely so they would reform and he would not have to use it.
buddhism.tie_back: Ashoka raises the rod as a warning and hopes never to strike, which is the Kural’s strategy.
buddhism.source: Ashoka, Rock Edict XIII (trans. S. Dhammika)
buddhism._accuracy_note: Very close in logic; Ashoka’s motive is Buddhist remorse and non-injury rather than long prosperity.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In Aeschylus’ Eumenides, Athena founds the Areopagus court and tells the Athenians to honour neither anarchy nor despotism, yet not to banish fear entirely from the city; the terrifying Furies are then given an honoured, gentler role as the Kindly Ones.
greek_mythology.explanation: The myth keeps a measure of awe in the city’s justice but transforms raw vengeance into a restrained, protective institution.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Keep the dread in reserve, soften its actual use: this is the Kural’s raised rod and gentle stroke.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Good fit for balancing awe and restraint; the setting is the founding of a court, not a king’s sentencing.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Machiavelli advises that a prince should make himself feared in such a way that, even if he does not win love, he avoids hatred, chiefly by keeping his hands off his subjects’ property and not being needlessly cruel.
philosophy.explanation: Even the most hard-headed theorist of power holds that the ruler’s severity must be displayed but kept within bounds, or it will destroy him.
philosophy.tie_back: Machiavelli and Valluvar reach the same practical conclusion by different moral routes: show sternness, avoid actual cruelty, and your rule will last.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Paraphrase; Machiavelli prefers fear to love when forced to choose, which is more hard-edged than the Kural.

kurals.tamil:
வெருவந்த செய்தொழுகும் வெங்கோல னாயின்
ஒருவந்தம் ஒல்லைக் கெடும்.
kurals.transliteration:
Veruvandha seydhozhugum vengoalan aayin
Oruvandham ollaik kedum.
kurals.meaning: A cruel-sceptred king who habitually does things that fill his people with dread will certainly and swiftly be ruined.
kurals.elementary: Imagine a team captain who yells and scares everyone all the time. Soon nobody wants to play for them, and the team falls apart. The kural says a ruler who keeps people frightened will quickly lose everything.
kurals.university: This couplet supplies the chapter’s title phrase: வெருவந்த செய்து ஒழுகும் describes a ruler whose habitual conduct (ஒழுகுதல், ongoing practice) is to do dread-inducing things. வெங்கோலன், the ‘hot’ or cruel sceptre, is the opposite of the செங்கோல் (straight sceptre) of chapter 55. ஒருவந்தம் means ‘certainly, without doubt’ and ஒல்லை ‘quickly’, so the prediction is doubly emphatic: sure and soon. Commentators (Mu. Varadarasanar, Pappaiah, Kalaignar) agree in glossing ‘veru’ as the fear felt by the subjects (குடிகள் அஞ்சும்படி). The couplet is read identically in both sources consulted.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “He is the best of kings in whose dominions men live fearlessly like sons in the house of their sire.”
hinduism.explanation: Bhishma tells Yudhishthira that the mark of the ideal king is that his subjects live without fear, like children at home.
hinduism.tie_back: Bhishma states positively what the Kural states negatively: rule without dread is the standard, and rule by dread is ruin.
hinduism.source: Mahabharata, Shanti Parva, Section LVII (trans. K. M. Ganguli)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Direct thematic match on fearless subjects; the swift-ruin consequence appears elsewhere in the section.

christianity.quote_or_event: “For rulers are not a terror to good works, but to the evil.”
christianity.explanation: Paul describes legitimate authority as something that only wrongdoers need fear; ordinary good people should not live in dread of it.
christianity.tie_back: A ruler who terrifies the innocent has abandoned what Paul says rulers are for, which is the Kural’s tyrant.
christianity._accuracy_note: Paul defines right authority by whom it frightens; he does not predict the tyrant’s ruin as the Kural does.

islam.quote_or_event: “Indeed, Pharaoh exalted himself in the land and made its people into factions, oppressing a sector among them, slaughtering their [newborn] sons and keeping their females alive. Indeed, he was of the corrupters.”
islam.explanation: The Quran presents Pharaoh as the archetypal ruler who governs through terror, and whose power is later swept away.
islam.tie_back: Pharaoh’s reign of dread and its destruction is the Kural’s warning in narrative form.
islam._accuracy_note: Clear case of rule by terror; the Quran attributes his fall to divine judgment, not only to political consequence.

judaism.quote_or_event: “As a roaring lion, and a ranging bear; so is a wicked ruler over the poor people.”
judaism.explanation: Proverbs compares the oppressive ruler to a predator whose very presence terrifies the helpless.
judaism.tie_back: The roaring lion is the image of the வெங்கோலன் who rules by dread.
judaism._accuracy_note: Vivid match on terrorizing rule; the swift downfall is implied by the next verse (28:16) rather than stated here.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “All tremble at violence; all fear death. Putting oneself in the place of another, one should not kill nor cause another to kill.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha grounds non-violence in the plain fact that every being fears the rod and death, so no one should impose that fear on others.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural forbids a king to rule by dread; the Dhammapada explains why dread is a wrong to inflict.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Addressed to all people rather than kings; the Pali ‘danda’ (rod, violence) nicely echoes the sceptre image.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In the legend retold by Cicero, the tyrant Dionysius of Syracuse lets the flatterer Damocles sit on his throne for a day, with a sword hanging over his head by a single horsehair, to show that a ruler who governs by fear lives in constant fear himself.
greek_mythology.explanation: The sword of Damocles pictures the insecurity of a regime built on terror.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The Kural says such a ruler perishes swiftly; the legend shows the blade already hanging over him.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Legend rather than myth, and it stresses the tyrant’s anxiety more than his actual downfall.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “But, of all motives, none is better adapted to secure influence and hold it fast than love; nothing is more foreign to that end than fear.”
philosophy.explanation: Cicero, quoting Ennius (‘whom they fear they hate’), argues that no power can stand against the hatred of the many and that every despot meets a violent end.
philosophy.tie_back: Cicero’s case against ruling by fear is almost a prose commentary on this Kural’s ‘surely and swiftly ruined’.
philosophy.source: Cicero, De Officiis 2.23 (trans. W. Miller, Loeb)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Near one-to-one: rule by fear is self-defeating and the tyrant falls.

kurals.tamil:
இறைகடியன் என்றுரைக்கும் இன்னாச்சொல் வேந்தன்
உறைகடுகி ஒல்லைக் கெடும்.
kurals.transliteration:
Iraikadiyan endruraikkum innaachchol vaendhan
Uraikadugi ollaik kedum.
kurals.meaning: A king who earns the bitter name ‘our ruler is cruel’ from his people will have his span cut short and will quickly perish.
kurals.elementary: If everyone at school whispers ‘the new class monitor is mean,’ that monitor won’t be monitor for long. The kural says when a whole country calls its king cruel, his time is almost up.
kurals.university: The couplet turns from the ruler’s acts to the people’s verdict: இறை கடியன் (‘the lord is harsh’) is the இன்னாச் சொல், the painful word, that the subjects speak. The ruler is thus defined by his reputation, and public opinion becomes a political force. உறை கடுகி is glossed by Mu. Varadarasanar as ‘his lifespan shrinking’ (ஆயுள் குறைந்து), while Pappaiah reads it as the term of his rule contracting; both readings fit, and Pope’s ‘his age shall dwindle’ follows the first. ஒல்லைக் கெடும் repeats the ‘swiftly perishes’ of 563, binding the two couplets together. The text is the same in both sources.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “That king who through folly rashly oppresses his kingdom, (will), together with his relatives, ere long be deprived of his life and of his kingdom.”
hinduism.explanation: Manu warns that an oppressive king loses both his life and his throne before long.
hinduism.tie_back: The same double loss (shortened life, quick ruin) that the Kural predicts for the king his people call cruel.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Near one-to-one on consequence; Manu stresses the oppression itself, the Kural the people’s verdict on it.

christianity.quote_or_event: “The kings of the Gentiles exercise lordship over them … But ye shall not be so: but he that is greatest among you, let him be as the younger; and he that is chief, as he that doth serve.”
christianity.explanation: Jesus contrasts domineering rulers with the servant-leadership he asks of his disciples.
christianity.tie_back: The Kural condemns the ruler remembered for harshness; Jesus redefines greatness as service.
christianity._accuracy_note: Shared rejection of domineering rule; no mention of reputation or swift downfall.

islam.quote_or_event: “The best of your rulers are those whom you love and who love you … And the worst of your rulers are those whom you hate and who hate you and whom you curse and who curse you.”
islam.explanation: The Prophet measures rulers by the mutual regard between them and their people.
islam.tie_back: A ruler his people curse as cruel is ‘the worst of rulers’, the one the Kural says quickly perishes.
islam._accuracy_note: Strong on the people’s verdict; the same hadith forbids armed revolt, so it does not predict the ruler’s fall.

judaism.quote_or_event: “And the king answered the people roughly … saying, My father made your yoke heavy, and I will add to your yoke: my father also chastised you with whips, but I will chastise you with scorpions.”
judaism.explanation: Rehoboam rejects his elders’ counsel and threatens his people with harsher rule; ten tribes immediately break away.
judaism.tie_back: Harsh words and a reputation for cruelty cost Rehoboam most of his kingdom at once, just as the Kural warns.
judaism._accuracy_note: An almost perfect narrative illustration: harsh speech, people’s rejection, swift loss of power.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Speak not harshly to anyone, for those thus spoken to might retort. Indeed, angry speech hurts, and retaliation may overtake you.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha warns that harsh speech rebounds on the speaker.
buddhism.tie_back: The king whose harshness becomes a byword finds it returning on him as the people’s bitter verdict.
buddhism._accuracy_note: General teaching on speech and retaliation, not specific to rulers.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In Sophocles’ Antigone, Creon’s son Haemon warns him that the whole city is quietly mourning Antigone and condemning his harsh decree, but Creon refuses to listen and soon loses his son and wife.
greek_mythology.explanation: The Theban legend shows a ruler deaf to his people’s murmurs about his cruelty, and destroyed as a result.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Haemon reports exactly the ‘இன்னாச் சொல்’ the Kural describes, and Creon’s ruin follows swiftly.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Strong match on public verdict and swift ruin; Creon loses his family and happiness rather than his throne.

philosophy.quote_or_event: In Xenophon’s Hiero, the tyrant Hiero confesses that he knows he is hated, lives in constant fear, and cannot trust anyone; the poet Simonides advises him to win his citizens’ love by kindness instead.
philosophy.explanation: Xenophon portrays the tyrant’s life as shortened and poisoned by the hatred he has earned.
philosophy.tie_back: The ruler known as cruel lives under the shadow the Kural describes; Xenophon offers the same cure the chapter implies.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Paraphrase; stresses the tyrant’s misery more than the brevity of his rule.

kurals.tamil:
அருஞ்செவ்வி இன்னா முகத்தான் பெருஞ்செல்வம்
பேஎய்கண் டன்னது உடைத்து.
kurals.transliteration:
Arunjevvi innaa mugaththaan perunjelvam
Paeey kandannadhu udaiththu.
kurals.meaning: The vast wealth of a ruler who is hard to see and who greets people with a harsh face is like treasure guarded by a demon: frightening and of no use to anyone.
kurals.elementary: Imagine a huge toy box that belongs to someone who never opens the door and scowls at everyone who knocks. Nobody gets to play with the toys, so it’s as if a monster were sitting on them. The kural says a leader who can’t be reached and always frowns makes his riches useless.
kurals.university: Two faults are named: அருஞ்செவ்வி, rare or difficult audience (செவ்வி = an opportune moment of access), and இன்னா முகம், a disagreeable countenance. The simile பேஎய் கண்டு அன்னது is read in the commentarial tradition as wealth that a pēy (demon, ghoul) has seen or seized: it exists but inspires only fear and benefits no one, which is why Pope renders ‘blasted by demon’s glance’ and Pappaiah ‘held by a bhūta’. The couplet widens the chapter’s idea of dread from punishment to everyday demeanour: an unapproachable, scowling ruler terrifies without lifting a rod. The spelling பேஎய் preserves the classical alapedai (vowel prolongation) for metre, and both sources agree on the text.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “When in the court, he shall never cause his petitioners to wait at the door, for when a king makes himself inaccessible to his people and entrusts his work to his immediate officers, he may be sure to engender confusion in business, and to cause thereby public disaffection, and himself a prey to his enemies.”
hinduism.explanation: Kautilya makes accessibility a core royal duty, warning that an unreachable king breeds disaffection and falls to his enemies.
hinduism.tie_back: ‘அருஞ்செவ்வி’ (rare audience) is precisely the inaccessibility the Arthashastra condemns.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Near one-to-one on inaccessibility; the Kural adds the harsh face and the demon-treasure image.

christianity.quote_or_event: “There was in a city a judge, which feared not God, neither regarded man: And there was a widow in that city; and she came unto him, saying, Avenge me of mine adversary. And he would not for a while.”
christianity.explanation: Jesus’ parable describes a judge who has the power to help but will not hear the needy, contrasting him with a God who listens.
christianity.tie_back: The unjust judge who will not give audience is the Kural’s அருஞ்செவ்வி ruler.
christianity._accuracy_note: Good image of an inaccessible authority; the parable’s main point is persistent prayer.

islam.quote_or_event: “No Imam closes his door on one in need, dire straits and poverty, except that Allah closes the gates of the Heavens from his dire straits, his needs, and his poverty.”
islam.explanation: On hearing this, Mu‘awiya appointed a man to look after the people’s needs so that access would not be blocked.
islam.tie_back: A ruler who shuts his door is the Kural’s hard-to-reach king, and his wealth becomes spiritually useless to him.
islam._accuracy_note: Very close on inaccessibility; graded Hasan on sunnah.com.

judaism.quote_or_event: “And Absalom said unto him, See, thy matters are good and right; but there is no man deputed of the king to hear thee.”
judaism.explanation: Absalom stands at the city gate exploiting the fact that King David has become hard to reach, and so ‘steals the hearts’ of Israel.
judaism.tie_back: An unreachable king loses his people’s loyalty, which is the danger the Kural points to.
judaism._accuracy_note: Strong narrative parallel on inaccessibility; David is not portrayed as scowling or cruel.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “At any time, whether I am eating, in the women's quarters, the bed chamber, the chariot, the palanquin, in the park or wherever, reporters are to be posted with instructions to report to me the affairs of the people so that I might attend to these affairs wherever I am.”
buddhism.explanation: Ashoka deliberately made himself reachable at every hour so that the people’s business never waited on his convenience.
buddhism.tie_back: Ashoka is the historical opposite of the Kural’s அருஞ்செவ்வி king.
buddhism.source: Ashoka, Rock Edict VI (trans. S. Dhammika)
buddhism._accuracy_note: Excellent contrast on accessibility; the edict does not address facial demeanour.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Hesiod tells of the terrible serpent, offspring of Ceto and Phorcys, that guards the golden apples in a secret place at the ends of the earth, a treasure that no one may approach.
greek_mythology.explanation: The dragon-guarded hoard (later named Ladon) is wealth that exists but benefits no one, because terror surrounds it.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The Kural’s ‘wealth seen by a demon’ is the same image: riches made useless by the fearsome guardian sitting on them.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Captures the demon-guarded treasure image only; there is no ruler or subjects in the myth.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Aristotle advises that a ruler who wishes to preserve his rule should appear to his subjects not harsh but dignified, inspiring respect rather than fear, and should seem a guardian of the public treasury rather than its owner.
philosophy.explanation: Aristotle links the ruler’s demeanour and his handling of wealth directly to the stability of his rule.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural condemns the harsh face and the hoarded, unusable wealth; Aristotle recommends the dignified face and wealth held in trust.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Paraphrase; Aristotle is advising how tyrannies may last, which is a different framing from Valluvar’s ethics.

kurals.tamil:
கடுஞ்சொல்லன் கண்ணிலன் ஆயின் நெடுஞ்செல்வம்
நீடின்றி ஆங்கே கெடும்.
kurals.transliteration:
Kadunjollan kannilan aayin nedunjelvam
Needindri aangae kedum.
kurals.meaning: If a ruler is harsh in speech and has no kindly regard for others, his great wealth will not last; it will perish then and there.
kurals.elementary: A shopkeeper who is rude and never smiles at customers soon has an empty shop, no matter how many goods are on the shelves. The kural says a leader with harsh words and no kindness loses even great riches very quickly.
kurals.university: கடுஞ்சொல்லன் is one given to harsh words, and கண்ணிலன், literally ‘eyeless’, means lacking kaṇṇōṭṭam, the gracious, considerate regard that is the subject of the very next chapter (58, கண்ணோட்டம்). The couplet thus bridges two chapters: without kindly regard, even நெடுஞ்செல்வம் (vast, long-accumulated wealth) perishes நீடின்றி ஆங்கே, without delay, on the spot. Mu. Varadarasanar glosses கண்ணிலன் as கண்ணோட்டம் இல்லாதவன் and Pappaiah as lacking முகதாட்சண்யம் (considerateness), while Kalaignar renders it as a ‘merciless heart’. The contrast நெடும் (long) and நீடு இன்றி (without lasting) is a deliberate verbal play. Both sources agree on the text.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “Austerity of speech consists in speaking words that are truthful, pleasing, beneficial, and not agitating to others, and also in regularly reciting Vedic literature.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna counts gentle, non-agitating speech as a form of spiritual discipline (tapas).
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural’s கடுஞ்சொல்லன் fails exactly this discipline of speech, with worldly as well as spiritual cost.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Matches the speech element; the Gita frames it as austerity, not as a condition of lasting wealth.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Let all bitterness, and wrath, and anger, and clamour, and evil speaking, be put away from you, with all malice: And be ye kind one to another, tenderhearted, forgiving one another.”
christianity.explanation: Paul pairs the rejection of harsh speech with a call to tender-hearted kindness.
christianity.tie_back: The same two faults the Kural names, harsh words and lack of kindly regard, are what Paul tells believers to put away.
christianity._accuracy_note: Close on both vices; Paul does not tie them to the loss of wealth.

islam.quote_or_event: “So by mercy from Allāh, [O Muḥammad], you were lenient with them. And if you had been rude [in speech] and harsh in heart, they would have disbanded from about you.”
islam.explanation: The Quran tells the Prophet that his gentleness held the community together, and that rudeness and hardness of heart would have scattered it.
islam.tie_back: ‘Rude in speech and harsh in heart’ is almost a translation of கடுஞ்சொல்லன் கண்ணிலன், and the loss it brings is immediate.
islam._accuracy_note: Near one-to-one on the two faults; the loss is of followers rather than of wealth, though for a ruler these are the same.

judaism.quote_or_event: “A soft answer turneth away wrath: but grievous words stir up anger.”
judaism.explanation: Proverbs teaches that harsh words provoke hostility while gentle ones defuse it.
judaism.tie_back: The ruler’s grievous words stir up the anger that quickly undoes his fortune.
judaism._accuracy_note: Good on speech; the kindly-regard element and the loss of wealth are only implied.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “He who utters gentle, instructive and truthful words, who imprecates none — him do I call a holy man.”
buddhism.explanation: The Dhammapada counts gentle, non-cursing speech among the marks of the truly noble person.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural’s harsh-tongued ruler is the opposite of the Buddha’s gentle speaker.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Speech only; addressed to the spiritual life, not to rulers or wealth.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Ovid tells how King Erysichthon scornfully cut down Ceres’ sacred oak, ignoring pleas for mercy; the goddess cursed him with endless hunger, and he devoured his whole fortune until he was left with nothing.
greek_mythology.explanation: A proud, pitiless king sees his great wealth vanish almost at once.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Harshness and lack of pity destroy even ‘long wealth’ on the spot, as the Kural warns.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: The loss is a divine punishment for impiety, not the political result of harsh rule; a loose analogy.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Xenophon’s Cyrus holds his empire together by philanthropia, courteous speech, generous gifts and kindly attention to others, arguing that goodwill is a surer treasure than hoarded gold.
philosophy.explanation: The Cyropaedia presents kindness and pleasant speech as the true foundations of lasting power and wealth.
philosophy.tie_back: The positive image of the Kural: a ruler who is gentle in word and kindly in regard keeps both his people and his riches.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Paraphrase; Xenophon’s Cyrus is partly idealized and also calculating.

kurals.tamil:
கடுமொழியும் கையிகந்த தண்டமும் வேந்தன்
அடுமுரண் தேய்க்கும் அரம்.
kurals.transliteration:
Kadumozhiyum kaiyigandha thandamum vaendhan
Adumuran thaeykkum aram.
kurals.meaning: Harsh words and punishments that exceed all measure are a file that slowly wears away a king’s power to defeat his enemies.
kurals.elementary: A metal file rubs a little bit off a key every time you use it, until one day the key no longer works. The kural says that every cruel word and every too-big punishment rubs away a little of a leader’s strength, until it is gone.
kurals.university: கையிகந்த தண்டம் is punishment that has ‘gone beyond the hand’, exceeding its proper limit (Mu. Varadarasanar: முறைகடந்த தண்டனை). அடுமுரண் is the destroying strength, the capacity to crush enemies, and அரம் is a file, so the metaphor is of gradual erosion rather than sudden collapse, complementing the ‘swift ruin’ of 563–566. The couplet echoes 566 (harsh words) and 561 (proportionate punishment), making excess, not punishment itself, the target. The word தண்டம் (Sanskrit daṇḍa) links Valluvar to the wider Indian daṇḍanīti tradition of measured punishment. thirukkural-thamizh.org prints the sandhi form ‘அடுமுரண் டேய்க்கு மரம்’, identical in wording.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “If the king is not wrathful, if he is not addicted to evil practices and not severe in his punishments, if he succeeds in keeping his passions under control, he then becomes an object of confidence unto all like the Himavat mountains.”
hinduism.explanation: Bhishma teaches that freedom from wrath and from severe punishment makes a king as secure and trusted as the Himalayas.
hinduism.tie_back: The reverse of the Kural’s file: restraint builds the king’s strength where excess wears it down.
hinduism.source: Mahabharata, Shanti Parva, Section LVII (trans. K. M. Ganguli)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Close match on non-severe punishment and royal strength, stated positively.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Fathers, provoke not your children to anger, lest they be discouraged.”
christianity.explanation: Paul warns those in authority at home that excessive harshness breaks the spirit of those under them.
christianity.tie_back: Excessive harshness erodes the bond that gives authority its strength, as the Kural’s file does.
christianity._accuracy_note: Domestic, not political, authority; a next-best match on the harm of excessive severity.

islam.quote_or_event: “And the retribution for an evil act is an evil one like it, but whoever pardons and makes reconciliation - his reward is [due] from Allāh. Indeed, He does not like wrongdoers.”
islam.explanation: The Quran caps retribution at an equal measure and ranks pardon above it; going beyond the measure is itself wrongdoing.
islam.tie_back: ‘கையிகந்த தண்டம்’, punishment beyond measure, is what this verse rules out.
islam._accuracy_note: Strong on the limit of punishment; it does not speak of the ruler’s strength being eroded.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Forty stripes he may give him, and not exceed: lest, if he should exceed, and beat him above these with many stripes, then thy brother should seem vile unto thee.”
judaism.explanation: The Torah sets a strict upper limit on corporal punishment to protect the dignity of the one punished.
judaism.tie_back: The Torah forbids exactly the punishment ‘beyond the hand’ that the Kural says erodes a king.
judaism._accuracy_note: Direct match on limiting punishment; the rationale is human dignity rather than royal power.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “While being completely law-abiding, some people are imprisoned, treated harshly and even killed without cause so that many people suffer. Therefore your aim should be to act with impartiality.”
buddhism.explanation: Ashoka rebukes his judicial officers for excessive and unjust punishment, naming anger and cruelty as its causes and non-anger and patience as its cure.
buddhism.tie_back: Ashoka identifies and forbids the excessive punishment that the Kural calls a file on royal power.
buddhism.source: Ashoka, Kalinga (Separate) Rock Edict I (trans. S. Dhammika)
buddhism._accuracy_note: Strong on excessive punishment; Ashoka frames the harm as the people’s suffering rather than the king’s weakening.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “He repealed the laws of Draco, all except those concerning homicide, because they were too severe and their penalties too heavy.”
greek_mythology.explanation: Plutarch reports that Draco’s laws punished almost every offence with death, so harshly that they were said to be written in blood, and Solon swept them away.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Punishment beyond measure could not last; it wore away the authority of the laws themselves.
greek_mythology.source: Plutarch, Life of Solon 17.1 (trans. B. Perrin, Loeb)
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Athenian legal history rather than myth; a strong match on excessive punishment being discarded.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Seneca argues in On Clemency that frequent and cruel punishment does not secure a ruler but multiplies his enemies, since every execution creates new kin who hate him, while mercy makes his power safe.
philosophy.explanation: For Seneca, cruelty is politically self-defeating: it drains the ruler’s security instead of adding to it.
philosophy.tie_back: Seneca’s argument is the Kural’s file metaphor spelled out: excessive severity wears away the ruler’s strength.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Paraphrase; very close in argument, addressed to the emperor Nero.

kurals.tamil:
இனத்தாற்றி எண்ணாத வேந்தன் சினத்தாற்றிச்
சீறிற் சிறுகும் திரு.
kurals.transliteration:
Inaththaatri ennaadha vaendhan sinaththaatrich
Seeril sirugum thiru.
kurals.meaning: A king who does not think matters through with his counsellors, and then gives way to anger and lashes out at them, will see his fortune shrink.
kurals.elementary: Imagine a group leader who never asks the team for ideas, and then, when the project goes wrong, shouts at everyone. The team stops helping, and things get worse and worse. The kural says a leader who skips advice and then explodes in anger loses what they have.
kurals.university: The couplet is syntactically compact and has two established readings. Mu. Varadarasanar and Pappaiah take இனத்து ஆற்றி எண்ணாத as ‘not deliberating together with his circle (ministers)’, so the fault is failure to consult followed by angry outbursts; Pope, following the older commentary, reads it as handing affairs to ministers without himself reflecting, and then raging at them when things fail. On either reading the pattern is the same: neglect of counsel, then சினத்து ஆற்றி சீறுதல், being carried along by anger and flaring at subordinates. The result is that திரு (Śrī, royal fortune) சிறுகும், dwindles. Here ‘dread’ is directed at the king’s own ministers, extending the chapter’s concern from subjects to the inner court. The text is the same in both sources.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “From anger, complete delusion arises, and from delusion bewilderment of memory. When memory is bewildered, intelligence is lost, and when intelligence is lost one falls down again into the material pool.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna traces a chain from anger to delusion to loss of judgment to ruin.
hinduism.tie_back: The raging king of this Kural loses judgment in exactly this chain, and with it his fortune.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Strong on anger destroying judgment; says nothing about consulting counsellors.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Wherefore, my beloved brethren, let every man be swift to hear, slow to speak, slow to wrath: For the wrath of man worketh not the righteousness of God.”
christianity.explanation: James urges listening first and restraining anger, because anger does not produce right outcomes.
christianity.tie_back: ‘Swift to hear, slow to wrath’ is the exact reverse of the king who neither deliberates nor restrains his anger.
christianity._accuracy_note: Covers both listening and anger; addressed to believers generally, not rulers.

islam.quote_or_event: “And those who avoid the major sins and immoralities, and when they are angry, they forgive, … and whose affair is [determined by] consultation among themselves.”
islam.explanation: In consecutive verses the Quran praises believers who forgive when angry and who settle their affairs by consultation (shura).
islam.tie_back: Consultation and restraint of anger are the two virtues whose absence the Kural blames for the shrinking of royal fortune.
islam._accuracy_note: Both elements match closely; the verses praise a community rather than warn a king.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Without counsel purposes are disappointed: but in the multitude of counsellors they are established.”
judaism.explanation: Proverbs teaches that plans made without counsel fail, while those made with many advisers stand.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural’s king who does not deliberate with his circle is the one whose purposes are disappointed.
judaism._accuracy_note: Matches the counsel half; the anger half is absent from this verse.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “He who checks rising anger as a charioteer checks a rolling chariot, him I call a true charioteer. Others only hold the reins.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha praises the one who can halt anger as it rises, as a skilled driver stops a runaway chariot.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural’s king is carried along by anger (சினத்து ஆற்றி); the Buddha calls for the opposite mastery.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Anger only; nothing on counsel or royal fortune.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: At the opening of the Iliad, Agamemnon, stung by the seer Calchas’ advice, rages at Achilles and seizes his prize; Achilles withdraws from the war and the Greeks suffer disaster after disaster.
greek_mythology.explanation: A leader who answers counsel with fury alienates his best ally and brings losses on his whole cause.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Agamemnon is the Kural’s king who lashes out at those around him and watches his fortunes shrink.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Strong narrative parallel; Agamemnon did take counsel, but reacted to it in anger.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Seneca tells of the governor Gnaeus Piso, who in anger ordered a soldier executed, then, when the supposedly murdered comrade turned up alive, condemned the soldier, the returned man, and the centurion as well, turning his own error into three deaths.
philosophy.explanation: Seneca uses the story to show how anger in a ruler refuses correction and multiplies injustice.
philosophy.tie_back: Piso is the Kural’s ruler who does not deliberate, then rages at subordinates, to his own discredit.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a very apt anecdote; the loss is moral and reputational rather than financial.

kurals.tamil:
செருவந்த போழ்திற் சிறைசெய்யா வேந்தன்
வெருவந்து வெய்து கெடும்.
kurals.transliteration:
Seruvandha poazhdhil siraiseyyaa vaendhan
Veruvandhu veydhu kedum.
kurals.meaning: A king who has not prepared a place of defence beforehand will, when war arrives, be seized with fear and quickly perish.
kurals.elementary: If you never build a shelter and a big storm comes, you get frightened and soaked. The kural says a ruler who doesn’t prepare protection in peaceful times panics and falls when trouble arrives.
kurals.university: சிறை here means a protective barrier or fortification (Mu. Varadarasanar: அரண்), not ‘prison’ in the modern sense; the couplet is about defence made ready before செரு (battle) arrives. The striking reversal is in வெருவந்து: the very dread (veru) the tyrant inflicted on others now falls on him, so the chapter’s key word turns back on its source. Commentators connect this to the preceding couplets: a king who has alienated his people through fear and cruelty lacks the human ‘fortress’ of their loyalty when danger comes, which is why this apparently military verse belongs in a chapter on not ruling by terror. வெய்து கெடும் means ‘perishes swiftly/painfully’. Both sources agree on the text.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “That king, however, who is of righteous behaviour and who is ever engaged in attracting the hearts of his people, never sinks when attacked by foes. If overcome, he soon regains his position.”
hinduism.explanation: Bhishma teaches that the loyalty of a king’s people is his real protection when enemies attack.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural’s unprotected king falls in war; Bhishma names the protection he lacked: the hearts of his people.
hinduism.source: Mahabharata, Shanti Parva, Section LVII (trans. K. M. Ganguli)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Matches the chapter-level reading of the couplet (loyalty as defence) more than its literal fortification sense.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Or what king, going to make war against another king, sitteth not down first, and consulteth whether he be able with ten thousand to meet him that cometh against him with twenty thousand?”
christianity.explanation: Jesus uses the image of a king who plans before war to teach his followers to count the cost.
christianity.tie_back: Preparation before battle is exactly what the Kural’s doomed king neglected.
christianity._accuracy_note: Strong on preparation; the parable’s real subject is discipleship.

islam.quote_or_event: “And prepare against them whatever you are able of power and of steeds of war by which you may terrify the enemy of Allāh and your enemy.”
islam.explanation: The Quran commands the community to be prepared for defence so that aggressors are deterred.
islam.tie_back: Readiness before conflict is what the Kural’s king failed to make; notably, both texts direct deterrence at external enemies, never at one’s own people.
islam._accuracy_note: Good on preparation; the verse’s ‘terrify’ concerns deterring enemies, distinct from the tyranny this chapter condemns.

judaism.quote_or_event: “They which builded on the wall, and they that bare burdens, with those that laded, every one with one of his hands wrought in the work, and with the other hand held a weapon.”
judaism.explanation: Nehemiah’s people rebuild Jerusalem’s wall while armed, making their defences ready before the enemy strikes.
judaism.tie_back: A people who build their own wall willingly is the opposite of the Kural’s ruler without a fortress.
judaism._accuracy_note: Good image of timely defence built by a loyal people; no tyrant is involved.

buddhism.quote_or_event: When King Ajatasattu plans to attack the Vajjians, the Buddha says they cannot be defeated so long as they meet often in harmony, honour their elders, protect the vulnerable and keep their customs; Ajatasattu’s minister concludes they cannot be conquered by force.
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha presents a people’s internal harmony and justice as their strongest defence.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural’s king lacks a protective ‘fortress’; the Vajjians’ fortress is the goodwill and order of their society.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase; matches the chapter-level reading (social loyalty as defence) rather than literal fortification.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In the Odyssey, the bard Demodocus sings of the wooden horse that the Trojans dragged inside their own walls; with their guard down, Troy fell in a single night.
greek_mythology.explanation: A city that neglected its defence at the decisive moment was destroyed swiftly and completely.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Like the Kural’s king without protection, Troy was caught unready and perished quickly.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Loose parallel on unpreparedness; Troy’s fall owed nothing to tyranny over its own people.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “Furthermore, those who wish to be feared must inevitably be afraid of those whom they intimidate.”
philosophy.explanation: Cicero illustrates with Dionysius of Syracuse, who dared not let a barber near his throat, and Alexander of Pherae, who needed armed guards even with his wife.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural’s word வெருவந்து, the tyrant himself seized by fear, is exactly Cicero’s point.
philosophy.source: Cicero, De Officiis 2.24–25 (trans. W. Miller, Loeb)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Captures the reversal of fear onto the ruler; Cicero does not discuss wartime defences.

kurals.tamil:
கல்லார்ப் பிணிக்கும் கடுங்கோல் அதுவல்லது
இல்லை நிலக்குப் பொறை.
kurals.transliteration:
Kallaarp pinikkum kadungoal adhuvalladhu
Illai nilakkup porai.
kurals.meaning: A harsh sceptre that binds ignorant, unlearned men to itself as its helpers is the heaviest burden the earth has to bear; there is none greater.
kurals.elementary: Picture a bully who gathers other kids who don’t know right from wrong to help him push everyone around. That gang makes the whole playground miserable. The kural says a cruel ruler with foolish helpers is the heaviest weight the world has to carry.
kurals.university: The closing couplet names the social mechanism of tyranny: கடுங்கோல் (the harsh sceptre) பிணிக்கும் (binds, attaches) கல்லார் (the unlearned) to itself, meaning it draws in and relies on men without learning or moral training to carry out its will. The traditional commentary, followed by Mu. Varadarasanar, Kalaignar, and Pope (‘Tyrants with fools their counsels share’), reads it this way; Pappaiah’s gloss instead stresses a regime that punishes so as to terrify, propped up by those who have not studied the books of justice. பொறை means a load or burden, and the idea of the earth (நிலம்) groaning under wicked rulers is widespread in Indian thought. The couplet ties back to chapter 41 (கல்லாமை, lack of learning) and closes the chapter by showing that terror is never exercised alone. thirukkural-thamizh.org prints the sandhi-joined ‘கடுங்கோ லதுவல்ல தில்லை’, identical in wording.

hinduism.quote_or_event: The Bhagavata Purana tells how Mother Earth, overburdened by vast armies of demonic rulers posing as kings, took the form of a cow and went weeping to Brahma, who promised that the Lord would descend as Krishna to lift the burden.
hinduism.explanation: The myth pictures tyrannical kings and their forces as a literal weight the earth can no longer bear.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural’s ‘நிலக்குப் பொறை’ (burden on the earth) is the same image, applied to a cruel regime and its unlearned agents.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase; a striking match on the burden-of-the-earth image, though the Purana’s framing is theological.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Let them alone: they be blind leaders of the blind. And if the blind lead the blind, both shall fall into the ditch.”
christianity.explanation: Jesus warns that leaders without true understanding, followed by others equally unseeing, bring ruin on all together.
christianity.tie_back: A harsh ruler bound to the unlearned is a case of the blind leading the blind, with everyone falling.
christianity._accuracy_note: Matches the ignorance of the ruling group; the burden-on-the-earth image is absent.

islam.quote_or_event: “So he bluffed his people, and they obeyed him. Indeed, they were [themselves] a people defiantly disobedient [of Allāh].”
islam.explanation: The Quran describes Pharaoh deceiving his people into following him, and holds them responsible too.
islam.tie_back: A tyrant who binds the undiscerning to his service is the pairing the Kural calls the earth’s heaviest burden.
islam._accuracy_note: Good on tyrant and pliant followers; the ‘burden’ image is not in the verse.

judaism.quote_or_event: “For three things the earth is disquieted, and for four which it cannot bear: For a servant when he reigneth; and a fool when he is filled with meat.”
judaism.explanation: Agur lists things the earth itself ‘cannot bear’, including the unfit man who seizes rule and the fool who prospers.
judaism.tie_back: The earth that cannot bear a fool in power is the Kural’s ‘no greater burden on the earth’.
judaism._accuracy_note: Remarkably close on the earth-burden image and unfit rulers; the specific harsh-sceptre element is implied.

buddhism.quote_or_event: The Mangala Sutta names ‘not associating with fools, associating with the wise’ as the very first of the highest blessings.
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha places the choice of companions at the foundation of a good life.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural’s tyrant does the opposite, binding the unlearned to himself, and so becomes a curse rather than a blessing.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Paraphrased; addressed to individuals, not rulers, and silent on the burden image.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In a fragment of the lost epic Cypria, Zeus pities the Earth, weighed down by the countless and increasingly lawless race of men, and plans the Trojan War to lighten her burden.
greek_mythology.explanation: Greek myth, like Indian myth, imagines the Earth as literally burdened by human wickedness.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The Kural’s ‘பொறை’ on the earth has a direct Greek counterpart in Earth’s plea to Zeus.
greek_mythology.source: Cypria, fragment 1 (preserved in a scholium on Iliad 1.5)
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Matches the burden image only; the Cypria blames humanity in general, not tyrants and their agents.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Plato describes how the tyrant must rid himself of the brave, the high-minded and the wise, and is left to live among the worthless, hiring bodyguards from the worst elements, as a doctor purges the best and keeps the worst.
philosophy.explanation: For Plato, tyranny by its nature drives out good and learned men and depends on the base and ignorant.
philosophy.tie_back: This is the Kural’s ‘கல்லார்ப் பிணிக்கும் கடுங்கோல்’ analysed from the inside.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Paraphrase; a very close structural analysis of the tyrant’s reliance on the unworthy.
